Synonyms/Regional Names: Madar, Arka, Aak, Baro akanda, Apple of Sodom
Key Visual Identifiers: Large waxy oval leaves with whitish bloom; clusters of star-shaped white or lavender flowers with a central crown; contains thick milky latex.
Active Phytochemicals: Calotropin, calotoxin, uscharin, calactin, calotropogenin, cardiac glycosides, gigantin.
Core Bioactivity: Anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimicrobial, purgative, cytotoxic, Shothahara.
Primary Indications: Skin diseases, joint pain, asthma, rheumatism, toothache, abdominal pain, helminthiasis.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Latex applied topically; leaf poultice; root bark decoction; leaf extract with honey.
Standard Dosage: Root bark powder: 0.5–1g; Flowers: 1–2g; restricted use.
Toxicity Profile: Highly toxic raw; latex causes severe skin/eye irritation and blindness; cardiotoxic.
Adverse Reactions: Severe vomiting, diarrhea, bradycardia, convulsions, skin blistering.

Key Visual Identifiers: Feathery light green leaves; small round greenish-yellow fleshy fruits with six vertical stripes; crooked trunk.
Active Phytochemicals: Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid), Gallic acid, Ellagic acid, Emblicanin A & B, Phyllantin.
Primary Indications: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), dyspepsia, gastritis, hair loss, jaundice, anemia, Type 2 Diabetes.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Fresh juice, dried fruit powder (Churna), decoction, Murabba (preserve), pickled fruit.
Contraindications: Acute diarrhea, dysentery, iron deficiency (long-term high use).
Adverse Reactions: Hyperacidity if taken excessively on empty stomach.

Key Visual Identifiers: Smooth grey bark peeling in flakes; buttressed trunk; oblong leaves; 5-winged woody fibrous fruit.
Active Phytochemicals: Arjunolic acid, Tannins, Saponins, Flavonoids, Co-enzyme Q10, Arjunetin.
Primary Indications: Angina pectoris, heart failure, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, bone fractures, wounds.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Bark decoction in milk (Arjuna Ksheerapaka), bark powder, aqueous extract.
Toxicity Profile: Low toxicity; safe at therapeutic doses.
Contraindications: Severe bradycardia; not a substitute for emergency cardiac care.
Adverse Reactions: Mild constipation or flatulence due to high tannin content.

Key Visual Identifiers: Large lanceolate leaves; white two-lipped flowers with purple streaks in dense spikes; four-seeded dehiscent capsule.
Active Phytochemicals: Quinazoline alkaloids (Vasicine, Vasicinone), Adhatodine, Anisotine, Saponins, Phytol.
Primary Indications: Asthma, bronchitis, chronic cough, tuberculosis, malaria, dysentery, respiratory congestion.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Leaf juice extraction, decoction of roots/bark, infused tea, leaf powder.
Toxicity Profile: Safe at therapeutic doses; cytotoxic in very high concentrations.
Adverse Reactions: Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea at high doses.

Key Visual Identifiers: Large deciduous tree; greyish-brown bark; globular/ovoid fruits covered in fine velvety hair.
Active Phytochemicals: Gallic acid, Ellagic acid, Bellericanin, β-sitosterol, Tannins, Chebulagic acid.
Primary Indications: Constipation, cough, throat infections, eye disorders, hair health, digestive problems.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Fruit rind powder, part of Triphala formulation, decoction of roots/bark.
Toxicity Profile: Safe at standard doses; seeds may be narcotic.
Contraindications: Pregnancy, severe dehydration, dry cough/Vata conditions.
Adverse Reactions: Excessive use may cause loose stools or dryness of mouth.

Key Visual Identifiers: Distinctive zig-zag green fleshy stems; slipper-shaped red/pink flowers; thick succulent leaves; milky latex.
Active Phytochemicals: Diterpenoids, Lectins, Saponins, Euphol, Germanicol, Cycloartenol.
Primary Indications: Warts, ringworm, insect stings, scorpion stings, localized inflammation/swelling, asthma.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Topical latex application, leaf poultice, leaf tea (with extreme caution).
Standard Dosage: External application only; no standard internal dose.
Toxicity Profile: Latex is a caustic irritant; toxic if ingested.
Contraindications: Oral consumption without supervision, pregnancy, application on open wounds.
Adverse Reactions: Dermatitis, skin blistering, severe vomiting if swallowed.

Synonyms/Regional Names: Haritaki, Harad, Abhaya, Vijaya, Ink Nut
Key Visual Identifiers: Oval leaves with glands at petiole base; ribbed ellipsoidal woody fruit turning black when dry.
Active Phytochemicals: Chebulinic acid, Chebulagic acid, Corilagin, Gallic acid, Ellagic acid, Tannins, Anthraquinones.
Primary Indications: Chronic constipation, digestive weakness, ulcers, cough, asthma, detoxification, memory loss.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Dried fruit powder (Churna), decoction, Triphala component, fruit chewing.
Safe Vehicle/Anupana: Warm water, Honey, Ghee, or Jaggery (varies by season/Ritu Haritaki).
Toxicity Profile: Safe for long-term use; known as "King of Medicine."
Contraindications: Pregnancy, severe exhaustion, acute dehydration, children under 5 years.
Adverse Reactions: Mild abdominal cramps, dehydration if overused as purgative.

Synonyms/Regional Names: Bitter vine, Refugee Lata, Topani lata, Japanese Pith
Key Visual Identifiers: Heart-shaped leaves; rapidly growing vine; small white or cream-colored flower clusters.
Core Bioactivity: Hemostatic, Antimicrobial, Wound healing, Analgesic, Hepatoprotective.
Primary Indications: External bleeding (cuts/wounds), skin itches, insect bites, stomach ache, high cholesterol.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Fresh leaf juice or crushed leaf paste applied topically; aqueous extract.
Standard Dosage: Topical application as needed; 50–100mg/kg in experimental studies.
Toxicity Profile: Safe for external use; potential hepatotoxicity to livestock/humans if ingested raw.
Contraindications: Internal use without supervision, deep puncture wounds without cleaning.

Synonyms/Regional Names: Japa, Gudhal, Chinese Hibiscus, Shoe Flower
Key Visual Identifiers: Large trumpet-shaped flowers (usually red) with prominent central staminal column; serrated leaves.
Active Phytochemicals: Anthocyanins, Quercetin, Flavonoids, Mucilage, Vitamin C, AHAs.
Core Bioactivity: Hypotensive, Hair tonic, Emmenagogue, Anti-inflammatory, Astringent.
Primary Indications: Hair loss, menstrual irregularities, hypertension, dandruff, skin redness/ageing.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Flower paste for hair, petal infusion (tea), oil infusion, root preparations (TCM).
Safe Vehicle/Anupana: Water, Honey, Coconut oil, or Rosewater.
Adverse Reactions: May lower blood pressure excessively if combined with medication; mild stomach upset.

Synonyms/Regional Names: Gandhabena, Gavati Chaha, Ghash, Citronella grass
Key Visual Identifiers: Tall tufted grass; linear aromatic leaves; citrus scent when crushed; bulbous base.
Primary Indications: Digestive distress (flatulence, cramps), fever, common cold, fungal infections, anxiety, insomnia.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Infusion (tea) of leaves, essential oil extraction, steam distillation.
Standard Dosage: 1–2 cups of infusion daily; 1–2 drops oil (diluted).
Toxicity Profile: Safe as food; concentrated oil is a skin irritant.
Contraindications: Pregnancy (large doses), renal disease, hypersensitivity to grass oils.
Adverse Reactions: Skin rash (topical oil), dizziness, dry mouth.

Key Visual Identifiers: Glossy green leaves; five-petaled flowers (pink, white, or purple); cylindrical pod fruits.
Primary Indications: Leukemia, Hodgkin's disease, Diabetes mellitus, hypertension.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Leaf decoction, chewing fresh leaves (traditional/folk use), leaf juice.
Toxicity Profile: Highly toxic; contains cytotoxic alkaloids affecting bone marrow and nerves.
Contraindications: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver or kidney disease.
Adverse Reactions: Hair loss, nausea, neuropathy, bone marrow suppression (low white blood cell count).

Key Visual Identifiers: Serrated leaflets; small white honey-scented flowers; green to yellow bitter drupe fruits.
Core Bioactivity: Antimicrobial, Antifungal, Blood purifier, Antipyretic, Antidiabetic.
Primary Indications: Skin diseases (acne, eczema), intestinal worms, parasites, diabetes, gingivitis, malaria.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Leaf paste, bark decoction, seed oil, twig chewing (datun).
Toxicity Profile: Leaf/bark generally safe; seed oil toxic to infants; potential antifertility in high doses.
Contraindications: Infants, pregnancy, couples trying to conceive (spermicidal properties).
Adverse Reactions: Vomiting, metabolic acidosis (in oil overdose), hypoglycemia.

Synonyms/Regional Names: Miracle Leaf, Life Plant, Panfuti, Pashanabheda
Key Visual Identifiers: Fleshy succulent leaves with scalloped margins that produce plantlets; drooping tubular flowers.
Active Phytochemicals: Bufadienolides (Bryophyllin A, B, C), Quercetin, Kaempferol, Saponins.
Primary Indications: Kidney stones (urolithiasis), urinary tract infections, gastric ulcers, wounds, boils.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Fresh leaf juice, chewing raw leaves with salt, warmed leaves for topical application.
Toxicity Profile: Generally safe for humans; bufadienolides can be cardiotoxic to grazing animals.
Contraindications: Pregnancy (potential uterine stimulant), chronic heart conditions, severe renal failure.
Adverse Reactions: Nausea, excessive urination, potential heart rhythm changes in very high doses.

Key Visual Identifiers: Kidney-shaped leaves with notched margins; creeping stems rooting at nodes; grows in damp areas.
Active Phytochemicals: Asiaticoside, Madecassoside, Asiatic acid, Madecassic acid.
Core Bioactivity: Nootropic (Brain booster), Wound healing, Venotonic, Neuroprotective, Digestive.
Primary Indications: Memory enhancement, skin ulcers, varicose veins, dysentery, anxiety, stomach ulcers.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Fresh leaf juice, raw leaves in salads/mash, dried powder, pills with honey/ginger.

Key Visual Identifiers: Aromatic square stems; opposite serrated green or purple leaves; terminal purple flower spikes.
Active Phytochemicals: Eugenol, Ursolic acid, Rosmarinic acid, Methyl eugenol, Caryophyllene.
Primary Indications: Common cold, cough, respiratory infections, stress, fever, bronchitis, immunity support.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Leaf decoction (tea), fresh juice with honey, leaf chewing.
Safe Vehicle/Anupana: Honey, Warm water, or Ginger juice.
Contraindications: Pregnancy (large doses), surgery (potential blood-thinning effect), hypoglycemia.
Adverse Reactions: May lower blood sugar excessively; mild anti-fertility effect (reversible).

Synonyms/Regional Names: Sambung Nyawa, Sabungai, Diabetes Plant, Cholesterol Spinach
Key Visual Identifiers: Fleshy green leaves often with purple-tinged undersides/stems; yellow-orange flower heads.
Active Phytochemicals: Flavonoids (Kaempferol, Quercetin), Saponins, Tannins, Chlorogenic acids, Phytol.
Primary Indications: Diabetes mellitus, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, gastric ulcers, inflammation, kidney issues.
Traditional Preparation Methods: Raw leaves eaten in salads/smoothies, dried leaf tea, flash-cooked stir-fry, ethanol extraction.
Toxicity Profile: Considered safe as food; LD50 exceeds 2000mg/kg in rodent studies.
Contraindications: Pregnancy and breastfeeding (lack of data), Asteraceae/Ragweed allergies.
Adverse Reactions: Potential hypoglycemia if taken with insulin/diabetes meds; additive antihypertensive effects.
